summary: Introduces the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) architecture and its terminology. It also lists architectural, modeling and protocol requirements for logically separating the control and data forwarding planes of an IP networking device. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) divides network-device control from packet forwarding. RFC 3654 defines terms and requirements for the architecture, the model of forwarding functions and the protocol between the two parts.

questions: separation of control and forwarding planes
how does forces separate control and forwarding
subtitle: Architecture and protocol requirements for separating router control from forwarding.

tldr.problem: Network devices often combine control software and per-packet forwarding, which makes the two functions difficult to develop independently.
tldr.mechanism: ForCES separates Control Elements from Forwarding Elements and defines requirements for their architecture, the forwarding-element model and their communication protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3654 is an Informational requirements document. It describes goals for the ForCES protocol and model, but does not specify the protocol itself.

facts.label: Scale target
facts.value: At least hundreds of FEs and tens of thousands of ports

today: RFC 3654 is an Informational requirements document published in November 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets goals for ForCES but does not define the protocol or FE model.

sections.title: Control and Forwarding Elements
sections.content:
A network device can have logically separate control-plane and forwarding-plane components while appearing as one device to outside systems. The control plane runs routing and signaling protocols; the forwarding plane handles each packet.

In ForCES, a Control Element (CE) instructs one or more Forwarding Elements (FEs) how to process packets. A ForCES Network Element contains one or more CEs and FEs and presents a single point of management. The ForCES protocol covers communication between associated CEs and FEs.
sections.plainLanguage: The control element makes decisions, and forwarding elements process packets according to those decisions. Together they appear as one network device.

sections.title: Requirements for the Network Element
sections.content:
The architecture must let CEs and FEs connect using different interconnect technologies, and a packet must be able to enter through one FE and leave through another. The network element must appear as one functional device; for example, a router decrements a packet's TTL only once as it passes through the element.

The architecture must support CE redundancy and failover, dynamic joining and leaving of CEs and FEs, and scale to at least hundreds of FEs and tens of thousands of ports. It must also let forwarding elements report changes and redirect control packets to their control element.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate components must still behave like one device and allow traffic to cross between forwarding elements. The architecture must support component failure and growth to the scale stated in the RFC.

sections.title: The Forwarding Element Model
sections.content:
A CE needs to know how an FE processes packets, so the RFC requires a forwarding-element model that describes logical packet-processing functions. The model must describe both the capabilities an FE offers and its current configuration.

The model must allow different implementations and ordering of functions, including repeated instances of the same function. Its minimal expressible set includes ports, IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding, quality-of-service functions, filtering, tunneling, encryption and asynchronous off-loaded functions; this does not require every FE to provide every function.
sections.plainLanguage: The model tells a control element what a forwarding element can do and how it is configured. It describes possible functions without requiring every forwarding element to support them all.

sections.title: Requirements for the ForCES Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol must let a CE discover FE capabilities, configure entries and parameters, query statistics, and receive events. It must support both redirection, which stops further FE processing, and mirroring, which sends a copy to the CE while the original continues.

The requirements also cover command bundling, message priority, dynamic association, topology exchange and CE failover. Information such as forwarding tables must be delivered reliably, while some redirected packets or heartbeat messages need not require strict reliability. Across multiple IP hops, the protocol uses a transport with adequate reliability, security and congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol carries configuration and status between control and forwarding elements. It needs reliable delivery for critical settings and can use less strict delivery for some time-sensitive messages.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The architecture must prevent unauthorized elements from joining a network element. The protocol must support message integrity, privacy and authentication of CEs and FEs.

When CEs and FEs communicate inside one secured box over a backplane, the architecture may rely on the box's physical security. When they communicate over a network, the RFC requires security mechanisms to be specified or selected.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized control and forwarding elements should join. Network connections need security mechanisms to protect messages and verify participants.
